causalMechanism.primaryVector: Chronic nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) therapy injures the esophageal mucosa and promotes reflux disease through inhibition of cyclooxygenase-1-mediated prostaglandin synthesis and direct topical injury. Prostaglandins maintain mucosal blood flow, bicarbonate and mucus secretion, epithelial restitution, and mucosal immunoregulation throughout the upper gastrointestinal tract; their depletion leaves the esophageal epithelium vulnerable to acid-pepsin injury, while the weakly acidic NSAID molecule itself can cause topical injury during reflux episodes (the mechanism of action proposed in the case-control literature for NSAID-associated esophageal ulceration). Because many patients with service-connected osteoarthritis take NSAIDs continuously for years, the exposure is typically prolonged and often combined with other reflux risk factors (hiatus hernia, obesity, smoking, age), producing an additive risk profile. The population evidence is direct: a prospective case-control study of 195 patients receiving continuous NSAIDs for osteoarthritis found endoscopically diagnosed esophagitis in 41 patients (21%), with hiatus hernia (OR 3.72, 95% CI 1.63-8.49) and younger age (OR 1.79 per decade, 95% CI 1.11-2.86) increasing risk, and heartburn was reported by all esophagitis patients (OR 4.78, 95% CI 2.04-11); a meta-analysis of 102 population-based studies (460,984 subjects) found NSAID/aspirin users had modestly but significantly higher odds of gastro-oesophageal reflux symptoms (OR 1.44, 95% CI 1.10-1.88); and a mechanism review documents esophagitis among the upper gastrointestinal adverse effects of COX-1 inhibition by NSAIDs and aspirin. Under 38 CFR § 3.310(a), a disability proximately due to or resulting from the treatment of a service-connected condition is itself service-connected, so endoscopically documented GERD or reflux esophagitis arising on documented chronic NSAID therapy for service-connected osteoarthritis is a treatment-complication secondary claim; where reflux disease predates the NSAID exposure, § 3.310(b) limits service connection to the attributable aggravation measured against the baseline. For an 'at least as likely as not' opinion, document the specific NSAID, dose, duration, and adherence; endoscopic or clinically documented reflux disease with symptom chronology relative to NSAID initiation; and address competing causes — hiatus hernia and other anatomic factors, obesity, smoking, alcohol, pregnancy, scleroderma or other motility disorders, and proton-pump inhibitor or other acid-suppression history. Rating under DC 7206 requires the documented stricture/dysphagia and treatment picture specified by the schedule; uncomplicated reflux disease is evaluated under the applicable criteria in § 4.114 or by analogy under § 4.20.

causalMechanism.primaryVector: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs cause peptic ulcers by inhibiting cyclooxygenase-1 and thereby depleting the prostaglandins that protect the gastroduodenal mucosa: prostaglandin E2 and prostacyclin normally stimulate mucus and bicarbonate secretion, increase mucosal blood flow, and drive epithelial repair, so their loss leaves the mucosa vulnerable to acid and pepsin; NSAIDs are also weak acids that trap in parietal cells and cause direct topical injury, and both mechanisms together produce erosions and ulcers, most often in the stomach and duodenum. Importantly for claims, the injury occurs at therapeutic analgesic doses used for musculoskeletal pain, can occur without warning symptoms, and is the leading medication-related cause of ulcer bleeding. The quantitative evidence is strong: a meta-analysis of 25 studies found uncomplicated peptic-ulcer disease significantly more common in NSAID takers than in controls (35.8% vs 8.3%), with NSAID use increasing the risk of peptic ulcer approximately 3.55-fold and of ulcer bleeding 4.85-fold, and a synergistic interaction when Helicobacter pylori infection coexists; a separate meta-analysis of peptic-ulcer risk factors attributed 24% of peptic-ulcer disease in the general population to NSAIDs; and current Cochrane evidence frames the entire class of NSAID-induced ulcers as a recognized, preventable entity for which proton-pump inhibitors are the standard protective therapy. Under 38 CFR § 3.310(a), a disability proximately due to or resulting from the treatment of a service-connected condition is itself service-connected, so peptic ulcer disease developing on documented chronic NSAID therapy for service-connected osteoarthritis is a treatment-complication secondary claim; where pre-existing ulcer disease is documented, § 3.310(b) limits service connection to the attributable aggravation. For an 'at least as likely as not' opinion, document the NSAID regimen (agent, dose, duration, dates, over-the-counter use), the endoscopic or imaging diagnosis (DC 7304 requires endoscopic or imaging documentation where rated at 0 percent, and the evaluation above that level follows symptom burden), the chronology of NSAID exposure relative to ulcer diagnosis, and treatment; and exclude competing causes — Helicobacter pylori infection (test and treat), alcohol and smoking, physiologic stress and critical illness, corticosteroid co-therapy, Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, and gastric malignancy (with ulcer symptoms requiring biopsy at endoscopy where indicated). Where the veteran also has service-connected GERD evaluated under DC 7206, § 4.14 bars using the same signs and symptoms under both codes.
